title: Compromise of 1877
summary: The Compromise of 1877 was an informal cross-party U.S. political agreement struck in 1877 to resolve the disputed 1876 presidential election. Negotiated by Republican and Democratic leaders, it granted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes the presidency in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the last Reconstruction-era Southern states. It formally ended the Reconstruction era, enabling Southern states to roll back hard-won Black civil rights protections for nearly a century.

title: Hopi
summary: The Hopi are an Indigenous Pueblo people who have inhabited their ancestral homelands in present-day northern Arizona since c. 1490, existing continuously to the present day. A sedentary, maize-farming society, they retained their distinct spiritual and communal traditions despite centuries of Spanish and U.S. colonial encroachment. They remain a leading voice for tribal sovereignty, preserving one of North America’s oldest continuously operating Indigenous cultures.

title: Reconstruction
summary: Reconstruction was the 1865–1877 post-Civil War U.S. federal period that reintegrated former Confederate states into the Union and secured rights for newly freed Black Americans. Launched after the Union’s Civil War victory, it relied on federal legislation and Southern military occupation, facing violent white supremacist backlash. It established foundational civil rights precedents that fueled the 20th-century civil rights movement, marking a defining turning point in American racial history.

title: Jim Crow laws
summary: Jim Crow laws were a series of state and local racial segregation statutes enforced across the U.S. South from 1877 to 1965. Enacted after Reconstruction ended to entrench white supremacy, they forced racial separation in public spaces, schools, and transportation while systematically disenfranchising Black Americans. Their formal elimination via the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act represented a landmark core victory of the American civil rights movement.

title: Oʼodham
summary: The Oʼodham are an Indigenous group native to the U.S.-Mexico border Sonoran Desert, with a continuous presence in the region since at least 1490 that persists today. Comprising Tohono O’odham and Akimel O’odham sub-groups, they sustained traditional desert farming for centuries despite 17th-century colonial land dispossession. They now lead Indigenous water and land stewardship efforts, advancing tribal sovereignty across the American Southwest.

title: Caddo
summary: The Caddo are a group of Indigenous North American peoples centered in the present-day south-central U.S., with a continuous presence dating to before 1490, persisting to the current day. They built complex agricultural and trade societies, encountering European colonizers in the 16th century while defending their ancestral territories. As a federally recognized tribal nation, they advance Indigenous sovereignty and preserve their distinct ancestral cultural heritage.

title: Andrew Carnegie
summary: Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist who dominated the U.S. steel industry from 1873 to 1901. Building his Carnegie Steel Company via vertical integration during the Second Industrial Revolution, he undercut rivals to amass one of the era’s largest fortunes. His "Gospel of Wealth" essay and massive charitable gifts set a permanent model for American corporate philanthropy, while his 1901 company sale formed the U.S. Steel Corporation.

title: Karankawa
summary: The Karankawa are a group of Indigenous peoples who have inhabited the U.S. Texas Gulf Coast since at least 1490. Originally a nomadic fishing and foraging society, they faced violent dispossession from European and Anglo-American settlers that erased most of their traditional culture. Today, surviving descendants fight for federal tribal recognition, embodying ongoing Indigenous sovereignty struggles in the U.S.

title: Ojibwe
summary: The Ojibwe, also called Chippewa, are a major Indigenous Anishinaabe nation whose ancestral homelands span the U.S. and Canadian Great Lakes region, active from c. 1490 to the present. They developed early regional trade networks, later allying with French fur traders while resisting centuries of European American settler encroachment on their lands. Today they are a leading voice in Native American tribal sovereignty and cultural preservation efforts across North America.

title: Ho-Chunk
summary: The Ho-Chunk, also historically referred to as the Winnebago, are an Indigenous North American tribe continuously residing in the U.S. Upper Midwest from 1490 to the present. Targeted by 19th-century federal forced removal policies, the tribe later secured formal federal recognition and retained core land and cultural holdings in their traditional homelands. They remain a leading voice in modern Indigenous sovereignty and cultural preservation movements across the U.S.

title: John D. Rockefeller
summary: John D. Rockefeller was an American industrialist and philanthropist active from 1870 to 1911, best known for founding the Standard Oil Company. He built Standard Oil into a near-monopolistic trust that controlled 90% of U.S. oil refining, using vertical integration to outcompete and absorb rival firms. The 1911 Supreme Court order to break up his trust set a landmark precedent for federal antitrust regulation, while his charitable gifts shaped modern American philanthropy.

title: Potawatomi
summary: The Potawatomi are an Algonquian-speaking Indigenous North American nation occupying the Great Lakes region from 1490 to the present. Long focused on sustainable farming and intertribal trade, they endured 19th-century federal forced removal policies that displaced most of the nation to scattered U.S. reservations. Their modern sovereignty and cultural revitalization efforts have strengthened Indigenous treaty rights advocacy nationwide.

title: Menominee
summary: The Menominee are an Indigenous Algonquian tribe that has occupied the U.S. northern Great Lakes region, centered in modern Wisconsin, since at least 1490. Long reliant on forest resources and wild rice, they faced 19th-century federal land dispossession and briefly lost federal recognition in the mid-20th century before restoring their sovereign status in 1973. Their successful campaign to reverse termination policies established a critical precedent for Native American self-determination across the United States.

title: Standard Oil
summary: Standard Oil was a dominant U.S. oil refining corporation founded in 1870 by John D. Rockefeller in Cleveland, Ohio. Through ruthless horizontal integration that absorbed competing firms, it controlled roughly 90% of the nation’s refining capacity by the 1880s. The 1911 Supreme Court ruling that dissolved it as an illegal monopoly under the Sherman Antitrust Act set a landmark precedent for federal antitrust enforcement.

title: Miami
summary: The Miami were an Algonquian-speaking Native American nation historically centered in the Great Lakes region (present-day Indiana and Ohio). In the late 18th century, they led the Western Confederacy to resist U.S. expansion into the Northwest Territory. Following their defeat at the 1794 Battle of Fallen Timbers, they were forced to sign the Treaty of Greenville. This treaty was historically significant because it shattered Indigenous sovereignty in the region, ceded vast territories to the U.S., and paved the way for mass white settlement in the Ohio Valley, establishing a devastating precedent for federal Indian policy based on systematic territorial displacement.

title: Illinois
summary: The Illinois (Illiniwek) were a confederacy of Algonquian-speaking tribes historically located in the upper Mississippi River Valley. In the 17th and 18th centuries, their population collapsed due to European diseases and the Beaver Wars against the Iroquois. Their decline is significant because it facilitated French expansion, turning the surviving Illinois into crucial allies for the French fur trade, while illustrating the catastrophic impact of European colonization and inter-tribal warfare on Indigenous sovereignty.

title: Laissez-faire
summary: Laissez-faire was the dominant U.S. economic policy framework active between 1870 and 1900 that advocated strict minimal government interference in private industry. Emerging amid the Gilded Age’s explosive industrial growth, it rejected regulations on corporate monopolies and labor practices to prioritize unfettered business expansion. It generated unprecedented national wealth but spurred severe inequality, laying early groundwork for Progressive Era reform efforts.

title: Pawnee
summary: The Pawnee are a Plains Indigenous nation whose origins trace to 1490 in their historic homelands spanning central Nebraska and northern Kansas, existing as a federally recognized people to the present day. Originally a semi-nomadic agricultural tribe, they were displaced by European American settlers in the 19th century and forcibly relocated to an Oklahoma reservation. They continue to uphold their distinct cultural heritage, contributing to broader movements for tribal sovereignty and Indigenous equity in the United States.

title: Industrial Revolution
summary: The Industrial Revolution was a sweeping U.S. economic and societal transformation occurring between 1800 and 1900, shifting the nation from an agrarian, craft-based economy to one centered on mechanized factory manufacturing. Spreading from Britain, it leveraged steam power, domestic natural resources, and immigrant labor to scale production nationwide. It spurred rapid urbanization, fueled labor organizing, and established the U.S. as a leading global industrial power by 1900.

title: Osage
summary: The Osage are a sovereign Indigenous Plains nation based primarily in present-day Oklahoma, with roots in the central U.S. dating to before 1490, maintaining self-governance to the present. Forcibly displaced to an Oklahoma reservation in the 1800s, they retained communal rights to massive oil reserves on their land. The 1920s Osage Murders of tribal citizens for oil access spurred federal Indian policy reforms, cementing their legacy as a resilient, self-sustaining tribal nation.

title: Social Darwinism
summary: Social Darwinism was a pseudoscientific ideological framework popular in the U.S. between 1870 and 1900 that adapted Charles Darwin’s natural selection theory to human societies. Emerging during the Gilded Age’s rapid industrialization and westward expansion, it framed wealth gaps and racial hierarchy as outcomes of “survival of the fittest.” It justified unregulated corporate monopolies, U.S. imperial expansion, and segregation, shaping decades of discriminatory domestic and foreign policy.

title: Wichita
summary: The Wichita are a federally recognized Indigenous Great Plains nation originating in their ancestral homelands of Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas by c. 1490. Originally semi-nomadic agriculturalists with fortified villages, they endured 19th-century forced displacement and federal assimilation policies. Their modern tribal government in Oklahoma exercises sovereignty, centering cultural preservation and advancing tribal rights in U.S. federal policy.

title: Chinook
summary: The Chinook are Indigenous Northwest Coast tribal nations based in the modern U.S. Pacific Northwest, with a continuous presence dating to at least 1490 that persists to the present. They built extensive Columbia River trade networks and developed the cross-cultural Chinook Jargon trade language, enduring forced displacement from 19th-century American westward expansion. Today the federally recognized Chinook Nation continues to advocate for tribal sovereignty and the revitalization of its centuries-old cultural heritage.

title: Radical Republicans
summary: Radical Republicans were a faction of the U.S. Republican Party active from 1865 to 1877, during the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Composed of abolitionist-aligned northern politicians, they opposed lenient policies toward ex-Confederates, pushing for federal civil rights protections for formerly enslaved people. They secured passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, laying critical legal groundwork for the mid-20th century civil rights movement’s fight for equal rights.

title: Coast Salish
summary: The Coast Salish are a network of interconnected Indigenous peoples of the North American Pacific Northwest, whose societies have occupied their traditional homelands from c. 1490 through the present day. Their communities span modern southern British Columbia to northern Washington, with lifeways rooted in sustainable coastal resource stewardship and communal governance. Their ongoing activism for treaty and land rights has been a leading force advancing Indigenous sovereignty across the United States and Canada.

title: Gilded Age
summary: The Gilded Age was a period of U.S. history spanning 1870 to 1900, defined by explosive industrial, corporate, and urban national growth. Coined by Mark Twain to mock the era’s glittering elite wealth that concealed rampant political corruption, labor exploitation, and widespread working-class poverty, it set the stage for the early 20th-century progressive reform movement that addressed these deep systemic inequities.

title: Makah
summary: The Makah are an Indigenous North American tribe that has inhabited the northwestern Pacific coast of present-day Washington state since 1490. A traditional maritime whaling and fishing people, they faced centuries of U.S. federal encroachment on their treaty-guaranteed ancestral lands and cultural practices. Their successful legal battles to restore traditional whaling rights set a landmark national precedent for Indigenous tribal sovereignty and cultural survival.

title: Haida
summary: The Haida are an Indigenous nation whose ancestral territories span the Pacific Northwest coast of present-day Alaska, U.S., and British Columbia, Canada, with a continuous presence predating 1490. Famed for their maritime expertise and iconic totem art, they endured centuries of colonial dispossession of their traditional lands and resources. Their modern cultural revitalization and land back campaigns have advanced Indigenous sovereignty movements across North America.

title: Knights of Labor
summary: The Knights of Labor was an inclusive U.S. labor union founded in 1869, active until 1886. Originally a secret fraternal group, it organized nearly all workers regardless of race, gender, or craft, advocating for the 8-hour workday and an end to child labor. Though it collapsed after the 1886 Haymarket Riot, it pioneered cross-group labor organizing that laid critical groundwork for future U.S. labor movements.

title: Chumash
summary: The Chumash are a group of Indigenous peoples native to central and Southern California’s coast and Channel Islands, with a continuous presence from before 1490 through the present. They developed complex maritime societies, sustaining distinct cultural traditions through centuries of Spanish and American colonial disruption. Their modern land advocacy and cultural revitalization efforts have advanced Indigenous sovereignty and reshaped narratives of Native California’s enduring history.

title: "New South"
summary: The New South was an economic and social vision advanced by U.S. Southern leaders between 1877 and 1900, calling for the region to abandon its pre-Civil War agrarian, slave-based economy. Emerging after federal Reconstruction ended, its proponents pushed for industrialization and Northern sectional reconciliation while entrenching white supremacist Jim Crow laws. It reshaped regional economic trajectories while cementing the racial oppression that defined the South for most of the 20th century.

title: Ohlone
summary: The Ohlone are a group of Indigenous peoples native to California’s central coast, active from 1490 through the present day. They traditionally occupied lands spanning the San Francisco Bay Area to Big Sur, sustaining themselves via hunter-gatherer practices before 18th-century Spanish colonization that devastated their communities. Their ongoing land back and cultural revival efforts have emerged as a leading model for Indigenous sovereignty advocacy across the American West.

title: End of Reconstruction
summary: The End of Reconstruction was the formal conclusion of U.S. federal post-Civil War rebuilding efforts in the former Confederacy, finalized in 1877. Triggered by the Compromise of 1877 that resolved the disputed 1876 presidential election, it included the withdrawal of remaining federal troops from Southern states. It ended federal protections for Black Southerners, clearing the way for the Jim Crow segregation system that disenfranchised Black Americans for nearly a century.

title: Pomo
summary: The Pomo are a group of Indigenous peoples native to Northern California, whose continuous presence in the region dates to 1490 and extends to the present. Originally sustaining communities through fishing, foraging, and renowned basket-weaving, they endured violent land dispossession during 19th-century U.S. westward expansion. Today, their federally recognized tribal nations lead cultural revitalization and Indigenous sovereignty efforts across California.

title: Yokuts
summary: The Yokuts are a group of interconnected Indigenous Native American nations rooted in California’s San Joaquin Valley, active from 1490 to the present. Originally comprising dozens of distinct bands sharing a common linguistic family, they endured violent dispossession and mass cultural erasure during 19th-century American westward expansion. Modern federally recognized Yokuts tribes lead cultural revitalization and land advocacy, advancing broader Indigenous sovereignty movements across the United States.

title: Cahuilla
summary: The Cahuilla are an Indigenous nation of Southern California whose continuous presence in the region dates to at least 1490 and persists to the present day. They faced waves of Spanish, Mexican, and U.S. colonial dispossession that disrupted their traditional land-based lifeways and self-governance through centuries of expansion. Their ongoing land back and cultural revitalization efforts have advanced Indigenous sovereignty frameworks across the American Southwest.

title: Frontier Conflicts
summary: Frontier Conflicts were a series of armed clashes spanning 1763 to 1890, fought between white U.S. settlers, federal troops, and Indigenous nations across the expanding American West. They erupted amid relentless U.S. westward expansion, as the federal government seized Indigenous lands for settlement and resource extraction, prompting defensive Native uprisings to protect their homelands. These conflicts cemented U.S. control over the contiguous United States, while displacing hundreds of thousands of Indigenous people and causing lasting intergenerational harm.

title: National Grange Movement
summary: The National Grange Movement, founded in the U.S. in 1867 and active through 1880, was a grassroots advocacy group of rural American farmers. Formed in response to exploitative rail freight monopolies and predatory crop pricing that drained small farm profits, it lobbied for state-level regulation of transportation and grain storage. It laid early groundwork for federal farm policy and unified rural voters to challenge Gilded Age corporate power.
